newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Kandir says re-election helps reform.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kandir says re-election helps reform.

text.p: Brazil's reform program will be strengthened, not sidetracked, by an upcoming battle in Congress to give President Fernando Henrique Cardoso the chance of a second term, Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said.
"Once you approve re-election, you increase the probability of having deeper reforms in a shorter period of time," Kandir told Reuters in an interview.

The government expects Congress, which has so far failed to approve key reforms of the pension and tax system and civil service employment rules, would rally behind Cardoso were he given the chance to stand in the 1998 presidential race and remain in power until 2002.
"What's important are the reforms and they will be easier to approve in the re-election scenario," Kandir said.
A lower house committee is expected to hold a first meeting next week to begin discussing a proposal to allow Cardoso, and possibly state governors and mayors, the chance of a second term.
Backers of the reform argue Brazil and its newfound climate of low inflation and fiscal restraint need a break from the upheavals that accompany the handover of power.

However, some analysts have expressed concern the government may be tempted to relax its tight fiscal policies to muster support in the volatile Chamber of Deputies where the re- election amendment needs two three-fifths majorities.
Kandir denied there was any chance of a let-up in the government's crusade against inflation, which is at its lower levels for decades.

"Under no circumstances will we make allowances for the sake of re-election precisely because we recognize that President Fernando Henrique's strength has everything to do with low inflation," Kandir said.

The minister, who has emerged as one of the most vocal proponents of re-election, also played down speculation that defeat of the amendment would put a cloud over Cardoso's last two years of his term.

"In no way would no re-election threaten the Real or mean very weak growth," the minister said. "We're already on the path towards economic stability but...with deeper reforms, with more foreign investment, we could have stability with stronger growth."
Government whips have attributed the lack of enthusiasm among deputies for the government reform program to fears of losing votes in last week's first round of municipal elections.

After the second round of municipal voting on November 15, however, there are nearly two years before Brazil goes back to the polls and the government hopes discontents may return to the fold and vote for reform in the first half of 1997.
That support would be even stronger, the officials say, should Cardoso be given the possibility of power -- and the ability to reward congressional allies -- until 2002.
